_meta.description: Every term of art used across the dashboard — demographic, clinical, financial and policy. Written so someone who does not work in healthcare or insurance can read the research without a second window open.

terms.d: The three retirement spending phases, roughly 65-74, 75-84 and 85+. Go-go is peak discretionary — travel, leisure, elective procedures. Slow-go sees total spend fall while the mix rotates hard into healthcare and home services. No-go concentrates almost entirely in medical and long-term care. The terms come from retirement planning practice; this dashboard uses them as the master time axis.
The dashboard's master time axis: age-band populations projected forward. Every other panel indexes to it. The clock is why the thesis can make timing claims that a generic 'aging' narrative cannot.

The argument that aging is not one trade but a sequence of them, with a different beneficiary set every seven years or so. The handoff currently underway is from go-go (experiences) to slow-go (care).

Whether the population paying a given business is growing or shrinking over the thesis horizon. The core exploitable observation is that businesses with opposite gradients trade on the same 'aging' narrative.

The drawing down of accumulated savings in retirement. The crude version of the boomer thesis assumes mass decumulation causes an asset supply shock; this dashboard argues the wealthy largely do not decumulate — they die holding — and that the real effect is a change in the composition of demand.

The long-standing claim that a retiring cohort selling assets to fund retirement would depress asset prices. Repeatedly proposed since the 1990s and repeatedly not observed, because wealth concentration means the holders of the assets are not the people who need to sell them.

Required Minimum Distribution — the statutory obligation to withdraw a minimum amount annually from tax-deferred retirement accounts from a set age. Forces money out of the tax-deferred wrapper, but frequently into a taxable account rather than into consumption, which is why forced distributions are not the same as forced selling.

Registered Index-Linked Annuity — an annuity giving equity index participation up to a cap with a defined buffer against losses. The fastest-growing US annuity category and the clearest product expression of the behavioural shift limb A describes: households wanting equity upside with a floor.
An annuity crediting interest linked to an index with a guaranteed floor of zero. Principal-protected, which is what makes it the median retiree's product rather than the top decile's.

Converting a lump sum into a guaranteed income stream for life. Economically the correct solution to longevity risk and persistently unpopular with consumers — the gap between those two facts is limb A's opportunity.

The risk of outliving your assets, from the household's side; the risk of policyholders living longer than priced, from the insurer's. Reinsurers take the second deliberately, which makes them the professional counterparty to this entire thesis.
A corporate pension plan offloading its obligations — and the longevity risk inside them — to an insurer. A structurally growing flow driven by the same clock as everything else here.

Earning the difference between what you pay on a liability (an annuity) and what you earn on the assets backing it. The core economics of limb A's income-manufacturing theme, and the reason private credit and annuity origination have converged.
Registered Investment Adviser — a fiduciary advice firm, typically fee-based, independent of a brokerage. The channel limb B argues takes share at each transfer break point.
The large full-service brokerage firms with employee advisors. The incumbent channel that limb B says loses share when relationships are renegotiated at a transfer.

Holding client assets and providing the trading, reporting and administrative infrastructure for advisors. A structurally advantaged position because the custodian gets paid whether the advisor or the self-directed heir wins.

This dashboard's term for a moment when an advice relationship is renegotiated — a death, an inheritance, a retirement, an advisor's own succession. Limb B's core claim is that there are two per estate and that share moves at each.

The multi-decade passage of household wealth from the current holding cohort to spouses and then heirs. Commonly quoted at $80-100T over roughly twenty years; estimates vary by nearly a factor of two and are sensitive to asset-price assumptions.

Privately administered Medicare, paid a risk-adjusted per-member benchmark by CMS. Enrolment growth is pure cohort clock; profitability is set annually by CMS. The clearest single illustration of limb E's argument that demographics deliver the volume and government sets the price.
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services — the federal agency setting reimbursement rates across most of the care universe. The single most consequential counterparty in limb D.

CMS's winter publication of proposed Medicare Advantage benchmark rates and risk-model parameters for the following year. The tradable annual event for the payor vertical; the final Rate Announcement usually confirms it.
The mechanism adjusting per-member payments for how sick the member is. Changes to the risk model can move payor economics as much as headline rate changes, and are less widely watched.
Medical Loss Ratio — the share of premium spent on medical care. Both a profitability measure and a regulatory floor. Rising MLR is how limb C's wage inflation shows up on a payor's income statement.

Old-Age and Survivors Insurance — the Social Security retirement trust fund. Its projected depletion date is limb E's forcing function: depletion means benefits become payable only from incoming receipts, implying an automatic cut absent legislation.
The annual Social Security and Medicare Trustees publication containing the solvency projections. The single scheduled event that most moves limb E.
Contributing workers per Social Security beneficiary. Declining mechanically as the cohort claims. The fiscal-side reading of the same population table the cohort clock is built from.

This dashboard's shorthand for the step-function policy risk created by a date-certain trust fund depletion. Markets price step functions late and abruptly because the date is known but the content is not.

Skilled Nursing Facility — institutional nursing care, largely Medicaid-funded for long-stay residents and Medicare-funded for short post-acute stays. Census is driven by the 85+ population; margin is driven by state budgets and wage inflation.

Care after a hospital stay — inpatient rehab, skilled nursing, home health. Demand is driven by stroke, hip fracture and joint replacement recovery, three conditions that track the 75+ population almost mechanically.
Clinical care delivered at home under a physician plan of care, distinct from personal care. Structurally advantaged because it is cheaper than facility care and is what patients want.

Non-clinical assistance with daily living — bathing, dressing, meals, mobility. The largest and least glamorous category of aging-in-place demand, largely Medicaid-funded, and the position most exposed to immigration policy in the whole universe.
End-of-life comfort care, Medicare-reimbursed on a per-diem basis. Admissions are driven by deaths, which makes it the most forecastable demand curve in the care vertical.

Remaining in the existing home rather than moving to institutional care. The overwhelming revealed preference of the cohort, which redirects spend from senior housing toward home modification, in-home care and home services.

The anticipated release of owner-occupied housing stock as the cohort dies or moves into care. Real but slow, and far more geographically concentrated than the phrase implies — retirement metros first, not the national market at once.
Homeowners with legacy low mortgage rates declining to move because a new mortgage would cost far more. Suppresses turnover and is the main force delaying the silver tsunami.
Age-restricted housing for the 55+ market, typically amenity-led and independent — Del Webb is the defining brand. A go-go band product, which means the tailwind behind it has a visible expiry.

The spectrum from independent living through assisted living to memory care. An operating business dressed as real estate: its largest input cost is care labour, which is why limbs C and H collide inside it.
The National Investment Center's senior housing data — occupancy, rate growth and construction starts. The direct quarterly read on limb H's supply-trough thesis.
Specialised residential care for dementia. Highest acuity, highest labour intensity and highest revenue per bed in senior housing — and therefore the sharpest exposure to limb C's wage inflation.

Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement — treating aortic stenosis through a catheter rather than open-heart surgery. Converts an inoperable condition into a routine procedure for the very old, which is why it is the purest age trade in medical devices.
Device treatment of the heart's valves and chambers, as distinct from rhythm or vessels. Prevalence of the underlying conditions rises steeply with age.

Intraocular lens — the implant replacing the natural lens in cataract surgery. Premium presbyopia-correcting lenses are patient-paid above the reimbursed base, which is what makes cataract a private-pay age curve rather than a reimbursement-exposed one.
Clouding of the eye's lens. Effectively universal in those who live long enough, and the highest-volume surgical procedure in the age curve.

Revenue paid directly by the patient rather than by a government programme or insurer. This dashboard treats private-pay as a structural feature rather than a category — it is the escape route from limb E's reimbursement risk.
The risk that a government-set rate changes adversely. Structural rather than cyclical in this thesis, because limb E argues the political pressure grows precisely as limb D's volumes do.

The hypothesis that people stay healthy longer and spend a shorter period in poor health before death. Would push the entire care demand curve to the right, lengthen the go-go band and shorten the high-cost tail. Limb D's stated falsifier, and GLP-1 therapies are its live version.

The glucagon-like peptide-1 agonist drug class used for diabetes and obesity. The most plausible current agent of morbidity compression, and therefore the live form of the falsifier for the care-volume book.
Dementia and related conditions. Prevalence rises steeply past 80, making it the largest driver of long-term care cost and family caregiving burden in the no-go band.

The rising share of cremations versus burials in death care. Revenue per case is substantially lower, so operators must grow volume and premium service attach faster than mix erodes. The main structural threat to an otherwise certain demand curve.

Funeral and cemetery arrangements purchased and paid for in advance of death. Creates a large deferred revenue backlog that converts on a predictable lag, effectively pre-funding future volume at today's prices.
The hospice, funeral, cemetery and estate settlement chain. The one demand curve in the thesis that cannot be deferred, substituted or reformed away.

Known future demand meeting supply that was fixed by decisions taken years earlier — nursing school places, apprenticeships, senior housing starts. The strongest of the four reasons this thesis might not already be priced, and the only one that is directly countable.

The requirement that every limb answer why the market has not already priced a perfectly forecastable fact. Four candidate mechanisms are scored per limb: capacity lag, policy discontinuity, institutional lag, index composition lag. A limb that fails all four is a slide, not a trade.
The specific, observable condition that would retire a position or kill a limb, written down before the money is at risk. A falsifier that gets renegotiated when it trips was never a falsifier.

1 = watching, on the map. 2 = engaged, would own at a price. 3 = core structural position. Independent of froth — a name can be conviction 3 and froth 3 at once, which means right thesis, wrong price.

1 = insulated, price not extended. 2 = narrative priced, needs a pullback. 3 = crowded, priced for perfection. Deliberately separate from conviction so the dashboard can hold 'excellent business, no entry' as a single coherent judgment.

The under-saved majority of the cohort, as distinct from the top decile that holds most of the assets. Faces income adequacy and out-of-pocket care cost rather than estate efficiency, and is directly exposed to limb E policy risk. Two customers, two demand curves, tracked separately throughout.

The wealth-holding decile of the cohort. Consumes far below its income, does not meaningfully decumulate, and transfers rather than spends. The customer behind the trust, estate, luxury and legacy exposures.

Japan reached this demographic structure decades earlier and is the only real out-of-sample evidence available. It confirms the consumer basket rotation and contradicts the services-inflation claim — which makes it both the best supporting evidence and the standing challenge to limb C.
